lead: A CNC machine tool is a metal-cutting machine built stiff, so that motors can push the tool and the work along measured axes and the cut stays where the program put it. Two families cover most work: the turning centre spins the work and holds a turret of tools; the machining centre spins the tool and exchanges it from a magazine. Job shops making auto parts in Pune or pump shafts in Coimbatore buy one of these once batch sizes fall and drawings change every week.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for what the program does, and Unit 5, Metal Cutting and Machine Tools, for cutting force and spindle speed.

sections.h3: Two families: the work turns or the tool turns

blocks.text: A machine that turns the work is a lathe. Fitted with a program-driven turret, a tailstock and two controlled slides, it becomes a turning centre. The slides are X, across the bed, and Z, along it; X is usually programmed as a diameter, so the display matches the drawing. The bed is often slanted at 45° or 60° so chips fall clear of the ways. The turret holds 8 to 12 tools and indexes to the next in under a second. A tailstock supports long shafts. Add live tooling (small driven tools in the turret) and a C-axis that indexes the spindle, and the same machine mills flats or drills off-centre holes without a second setup.

A machine that turns the tool is a milling machine. Under CNC it becomes a machining centre: the spindle comes down from a column (vertical) or points sideways (horizontal), the table carries the work in X and Y, and Z feeds the spindle or the column. An automatic tool changer takes the next tool from a drum or chain magazine holding 20 to 40 tools. A pallet changer swaps a finished part for a fresh one while cutting continues, which is why horizontal machining centres suit boxy parts that need four faces. Five-axis machines add two rotary axes. CNC drilling and grinding machines are also built, for narrow single-purpose work.

sections.h3: Structure and guideways: hold still under load

blocks.text: Accuracy comes from stiffness, not from the controller. The bed and column must not deflect more than a few micrometres when the cutting force pushes back. Cast iron is the usual base: cheap to cast into ribbed shapes, and it damps vibration well. Welded steel bases are lighter, need no pattern and suit large one-off machines; they damp less, so they are sometimes filled with concrete.

Thermal symmetry matters as much. The spindle motor and its bearings make heat, and the column grows. If the heat sources sit symmetrically about the centre line, growth pushes the tool along one axis and the controller can compensate. If not, the spindle tilts and the error depends on height.

items: Dovetail and box ways slide metal on metal over an oil film: large contact area, good damping, but at very slow feeds the slide sticks and then breaks free — stick-slip.
Linear bearing carriages run on recirculating balls over a hardened rail: friction is low and stick-slip is gone, at the cost of damping.
Hydrostatic ways float the slide on pumped oil: no wear, fine for heavy loads, but they need a pump and a supply of clean oil.

blocks.text: A ball screw turns motor rotation into slide motion. A hardened screw and a nut carry recirculating steel balls between them, so the nut rolls instead of sliding. Lead is the distance the nut travels in one turn. Preload (two nuts with a shim between them, or oversize balls) removes play. Backlash is the lost motion when the slide reverses; the controller can compensate for it, but preload is the mechanical cure.

The spindle must deliver cutting power across a wide speed range. An older DC shunt motor is sped up by raising armature voltage up to base speed and by weakening the field above it; brushes wear out. A modern AC induction spindle runs from a vector drive, which holds the stator current in step with the rotor flux so torque stays high at low speed. A gear range or a built-in motor covers the top end.

blocks.where: v is the cutting speed in m/min, D is the workpiece or cutter diameter in mm, and N is the spindle speed in rev/min.

blocks.text: Feed drives move the slide and must also hold it still against cutting force. A stepper motor turns a fixed angle per pulse: 1.8° gives 200 steps per turn. No encoder is fitted, so the controller counts pulses and assumes the slide followed — open loop. That is cheap and simple, but an overloaded stepper stalls silently and every later position is wrong. A servo motor, DC with a tacho or AC permanent-magnet synchronous, carries an encoder and compares commanded with measured position — closed loop.

The drive must match the load. Slide mass and screw inertia are reflected at the motor shaft; if the reflected inertia is far above the motor's own, the loop is hard to tune and the slide overshoots or hums. Belt or gear reduction helps. Axis letters follow a standard: Z along the spindle, X the main cross axis, Y the third linear axis, and A, B, C rotate about X, Y, Z.
steps per turn = 360 ÷ step angle;  resolution = lead ÷ steps per turn;  feed rate = pulse rate × resolution
blocks.where: step angle is in degrees per step, lead is in mm per turn, resolution is in mm per pulse, pulse rate is in pulses per second, and feed rate is in mm/s.

examples.question: A stepper motor of step angle 1.8° drives the ball screw of a CNC table slide. The screw lead is 5 mm per revolution and the controller sends 2,000 pulses per second. Find the steps per revolution, the resolution in mm per step, and the feed rate in mm/s and mm/min.
steps: Steps per revolution = 360° ÷ step angle = 360 ÷ 1.8 = 200 steps.
Resolution = lead ÷ steps per revolution = 5 mm ÷ 200 = 0.025 mm per step.
Feed rate = pulse rate × resolution = 2000 pulses/s × 0.025 mm/pulse = 50 mm/s.
examples.answer: 200 steps per revolution, a resolution of 0.025 mm per step, and a feed rate of 50 mm/s, which is 3000 mm/min.
examples.check:
lead = 5.0
step_angle = 1.8
pulse_rate = 2000
steps_per_rev = 360 / step_angle
resolution = lead / steps_per_rev
feed_mm_s = pulse_rate * resolution
feed_mm_min = feed_mm_s * 60
print(steps_per_rev)
print(resolution)
print(feed_mm_s)
print(feed_mm_min)

traps: Lead is not pitch. Pitch is the gap between neighbouring threads; lead is the distance the nut moves in one turn. They are equal only for a single-start screw, and lead is twice the pitch for a two-start screw.
A stepper runs open loop, so nothing measures the slide and a stall raises no alarm. A servo drive with an encoder reports a following error instead.
A ball screw has low friction and is not self-locking: a vertical Z axis will drop when power is cut unless a brake is fitted. A power screw on a manual machine would hold.
On most turning-centre controls X is programmed as a diameter, so a 2 mm depth of cut changes the X word by 4 mm, not 2 mm.
The slant bed is for chip clearance and operator reach. It does not by itself make the machine more accurate — stiffness and thermal symmetry do.

quiz.q: Name the two linear axes of a 2-axis turning centre and state which one is programmed as a diameter.
quiz.a: X is across the bed and is programmed as a diameter; Z is along the bed, parallel to the spindle.

quiz.q: What does an automatic tool changer do on a machining centre?
quiz.a: It takes the next tool from a drum or chain magazine, fits it in the spindle and returns the used tool to its pocket, all under program control.

quiz.q: Why is stick-slip a problem on box ways at a feed of 5 mm/min but not at 200 mm/min?
quiz.a: At very low feed the slide creeps until the stored elastic energy in the drive overcomes static friction, then it jumps forward. The motion becomes a series of jerks and the surface shows marks. At 200 mm/min the slide moves fast enough to stay in the kinetic friction regime all the time.

quiz.q: Why is a ball screw nut preloaded?
quiz.a: Preload squeezes the balls between two nut halves (or uses oversize balls), so there is no free gap between the thread flanks. On reversal the nut does not move before it pushes, so backlash is removed and stiffness rises.

quiz.q: A stepper of step angle 0.9° drives a ball screw of lead 4 mm. The controller sends 3000 pulses per second. Find the resolution and the feed rate in mm/min.
quiz.a: Steps per revolution = 360 ÷ 0.9 = 400. Resolution = 4 ÷ 400 = 0.01 mm per step. Feed = 3000 × 0.01 = 30 mm/s = 1800 mm/min.

quiz.q: A slide cuts a 0.03 mm step every time the X axis reverses direction. The step repeats at every position and does not drift over the day. Identify the fault and give one test that separates it from thermal growth.
quiz.a: The fault is backlash. Approach the same point from +X and from −X with a dial indicator on the table: backlash shows as a repeatable gap of 0.03 mm at any position and any time. Thermal growth drifts as the machine warms, changes with spindle running time, and grows with distance from the datum.

quiz.q: A 5-axis machining centre costs much more than a 3-axis machine of the same table size. Give two reasons beyond the price of the two extra drives.
quiz.a: The rotary axes must hold their centre lines and offsets to a few micrometres, so the structure needs more stiffness, more careful assembly and more calibration. The controller must also interpolate five axes together, which needs a faster processor and more complex error compensation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production machines are moving to linear motors on the feed axes and torque motors on rotary axes: no screw, no nut, no wear, and higher acceleration. Polymer concrete beds are cast around steel inserts to raise damping well above cast iron. Thermal error is fought in software, by mapping the growth of the structure against spindle running time and compensating in the controller.
